title: Tenali Raman Tale 135

full_text:
A corrupt provincial governor named Jagannatha Rao sent a magnificent 'ceremonial tribute' to King Krishnadevaraya:
A miniature, life-size bullock cart crafted entirely of teakwood overlaid with embossed gold foil, pulled by two wooden bullocks with horns of pure silver.
Accompanying the cart was a letter from the governor:
'A humble token of my infinite loyalty, funded entirely from my modest ancestral savings!'

In reality, the governor had embezzled twenty thousand gold coins from the provincial road maintenance budget, leaving bridges broken and trade routes impassable.
The King was dazzled by the golden cart, preparing to promote the governor.

Tenali Raman inspected the golden cart.
He noticed that beneath the thin gold foil, the teakwood base was stamped with the official government insignia of the **Provincial Public Works Department**!

Tenali stepped before the King:
'Maharaj, Governor Jagannatha Rao’s loyalty is so extraordinary that he has offered to demonstrate the practical utility of his golden bullock cart today!'

Tenali had the golden cart hitched to two real, powerful palace oxen in the courtyard.
Tenali loaded the cart with fifty bags of heavy stone gravel from the broken city road.
Tenali then turned to Governor Jagannatha Rao, who was present in court:
'Noble Governor! Since you built this magnificent cart from your road budget, mount the driver’s seat and drive it across the main highway to Bellary to deliver these gravel bags to repair the broken bridges!'

The governor broke into a cold sweat:
'Master Tenali! This is a decorative ceremonial cart! Its axles are made of soft gold foil; if it carries heavy gravel across rough roads, the wheels will snap!'

Tenali replied with thunderous moral authority:
'Aha! The golden cart snaps under real gravel, just as your provincial roads collapsed because you spent the public road maintenance budget on gold foil to flatter the Emperor!
While you built gold carts for the palace, common bullock carts belonging to poor farmers are breaking their axles in muddy potholes on your neglected highways!'

An immediate imperial audit of the governor's province revealed that twenty thousand gold coins allocated for bridge repairs had been stolen.
The King stripped the corrupt governor of his post, melted down the golden cart to finance real road and bridge construction, and praised Tenali Raman:
'Tenali, thou hast turned a corrupt ornament into real roads for my people!'
moral: Public servants who accept lavish bribes disguised as ceremonial gifts find their graft exposed by fiscal reality.
